name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,347

entries.clue: Consume boring game bird as main course (5,4)

indicatorNotes.boring: To bore is to drill a hole straight through something, so one word is driven into the middle of another.

blocks.note: grouse are the moorland birds shot in Britain from the Glorious Twelfth of August
to consume food is to eat it

annotation.surface: A diner working through a dull game bird as the middle plate of a meal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Main course' is dinner on the surface and water underneath. The river runs through Buckinghamshire, Bedfordshire and Cambridgeshire to the Wash, the longest of the Ouses and the reason it needs its first word.
annotation.definitionFit: The Great Ouse is a major English river; a river runs a course, and 'main' is both chief and the old word for the open sea it runs to.

indicatorNotes.running: Something running has gone liquid and lost its shape, so the letters it describes will not stay where they were put.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters with the apostrophe ignored

annotation.surface: A dog owner reporting that the animal's nose is streaming.
annotation.walkthrough: The opening word looks like a possessive belonging to the dog and is in fact the whole definition, standing alone as an exclamation. A healthy dog's nose being wet is the picture that keeps you from seeing it.
annotation.definitionFit: 'My!' and the answer are the same startled exclamation — 'my goodness' puts both together, and either half on its own does the same job.

indicatorNotes.Cycling: Cycling sends letters round a loop: each moves up one place and the one that falls off the front goes to the back.

blocks.note: a den is the small private room at home where someone studies

annotation.surface: Reading up on bicycle racing and keeping at it to the last page.
annotation.walkthrough: Cycling keeps every letter and moves only the starting point, which is what separates it from an anagram. 'Study' wants the room rather than the reading.
annotation.definitionFit: To end and to finish are the same verb — bringing a thing to a close, or coming to one.

blocks.note: to hang about somewhere, staying longer than you meant to
a tar is a sailor, and the clue wants the adjective made from him

annotation.surface: Somebody hanging about the way a seaman might.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tar' for a sailor is old naval slang, from the tarred canvas and tarred pigtails of the sailing navy. The question mark admits the adjective is the setter's own, since the word normally means smeared with the stuff.
annotation.definitionFit: To tarry is to linger; and a sailor being a tar, the same word does duty for 'like a tar' — the question mark flagging that stretch.

blocks.note: the straight reading: taking in what is meant
the second reading splits the word after 'under': anyone in a chair that long is falling short of the standing he should be doing

annotation.surface: A suggestion that spending far too long in a chair is something one can sympathise with.
annotation.walkthrough: There are no letters to assemble here, only one word read twice. British English puts 'under-' in front of anything that falls short — underpaid, underfed, underdone — and the same prefix is hiding in a word about grasping things.
annotation.definitionFit: To understand is to comprehend; hyphenated as under-standing it describes doing less standing than one should, which is sitting down too much.

indicatorNotes.performing: Performing puts a piece on its feet and moves it around the stage, so the letters named do not keep the order they were printed in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

annotation.surface: A singer naming the opera they are currently appearing in.
annotation.walkthrough: Emporia is the Latin plural of emporium, the grand word a shop puts over its door when it wants to sound like a bazaar. The clue's own 'in' contributes nothing but a join.
annotation.definitionFit: An emporium is a large store selling goods of every kind, and emporia is its plural — shops on the grand scale.

entries.clue: Fight to have backside shaved in health resort (3)

indicatorNotes.have backside shaved: A backside is the rear of a thing, and shaving it takes the last letter clean off.

blocks.note: a boxer's practice bout, fighting without meaning to land anything; its final R is what the shaving takes off

annotation.surface: A struggle to get one's rear end waxed at a health resort.
annotation.walkthrough: Spa is a town in Belgium whose mineral springs gave English the word; the resorts borrowed the name afterwards. Boxers spar without meaning to hurt each other, which is the mildest fight the setter could have chosen.
annotation.definitionFit: A spa is where people go to take the waters or be pampered — the health resort itself, named for the Belgian town.

entries.clue: Small chocolate bar that gathers hair (9)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a relative clause saying what the object does rather than a noun standing in for it, which the setter allows himself because English has no one-word synonym for the thing.

blocks.note: s = small, the size printed on a clothing label
a Crunchie is a British chocolate bar with a honeycomb toffee centre

annotation.surface: A little chocolate bar that seems to pick up hair.
annotation.walkthrough: The Crunchie has been a British sweetshop fixture since 1929, and the whole brand name is wanted rather than a piece of it. The definition describes an object instead of naming one, which is why it reads as part of the joke.
annotation.definitionFit: It is a loop of elastic in a gathered fabric sleeve, and its entire job is bunching hair into a ponytail.

blocks.note: a = American, the standard one-letter label
Che Guevara, the Argentine revolutionary whose first name crosswords use for any rebel

annotation.surface: A wounded rebel from the United States.
annotation.walkthrough: Che arrives whenever a revolutionary is mentioned, and he is worth learning by heart. The definition is doing double service as noun and verb, since a place that aches is a place that hurts.
annotation.definitionFit: An ache is a dull, steady pain, so 'hurt' covers it either way round — what aches hurts, and a hurt is an ache.

indicatorNotes.Rum: 'Rum' is old slang for odd or peculiar — a rum do — and letters called odd are not standing in their right order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

annotation.surface: A jockey riding the famous steeplechaser exactly as he was told to.
annotation.walkthrough: Red Rum won the Grand National three times in the 1970s and is the best-known racehorse in Britain, which is what lets the setter break the name in half. Only the first two words are shuffled.
annotation.definitionFit: To order somebody to do a thing is to instruct them, and the past tenses match: what was ordered is what was instructed.

blocks.note: the bar across a cage or a henhouse that a bird sits on
the spiny freshwater fish of European rivers and lakes

annotation.surface: A pole on offer for either a bird or a fish.
annotation.walkthrough: Rod is a third name for the same old land measure of five and a half yards, so the first word carries a sense the clue never needs. The fish and the roost are unrelated words that reached English by different roads and ended up spelt alike.
annotation.definitionFit: It is the bar a bird roosts on, and also the striped freshwater fish an angler lands — two separate words that happen to be written the same.

entries.clue: Quick! New one pence extremely pretty (5)

indicatorNotes.extremely: The extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the first and last letters of the word beside it are taken.

blocks.note: n = new, the label a relaunched product carries
i = one, the Roman numeral
p = pence, the mark on British coins since decimalisation
the outermost letters of PRETTY

annotation.surface: Somebody excitedly pointing out a brand-new penny and a handsome one at that.
annotation.walkthrough: Four pieces make a five-letter answer, three of them single letters, so the chain is nearly as long as the word. The exclamation mark is part of the definition rather than excitement in the scene.
annotation.definitionFit: Nippy is British for quick and light on the move — a nippy little car, a nippy winger — which is the briskness 'Quick!' calls for.

entries.clue: Parcel Pip destroyed is stationery item (5,4)

indicatorNotes.destroyed: What is destroyed has been broken up, and the pieces go back together in a different arrangement.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

annotation.surface: A parcel that somebody called Pip has torn to bits.
annotation.walkthrough: Pip reads as a name — Dickens gave it to the boy in Great Expectations — and that is the only reason it sits next to a parcel. Both words are fodder, and the answer's own gap is ignored.
annotation.definitionFit: It is the bent loop of wire that holds sheets of paper together, sold in every stationer's beside the staples and envelopes.

entries.clue: Central members of errant gang enthusiastic (6)

indicatorNotes.Central members of: The central members of a word are the letters at its middle, taken once both ends have been dropped.

blocks.note: the two letters at the middle of ERRANT, with ER and NT stripped off the ends
a ring is an organised gang — a drugs ring, a smuggling ring

annotation.surface: The core membership of a gang that has gone astray.
annotation.walkthrough: Only the first word is cut down; the second is swapped whole for a synonym, and that change of method halfway through is the join most solvers miss. The answer survives in modern English almost only in the phrase 'raring to go'.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody raring to go is straining at the leash to start, which is enthusiasm at its most impatient.

indicatorNotes.rocks: To rock a thing is to shake it about, and what is shaken does not settle back in the order it started in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: The barest stretch of rock creeping in on the land around it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rocks' is a noun in the picture and a verb in the machinery, and that swap is all that hides the anagram. The answer is the word the Lord's Prayer uses for a sin as well as the one a landowner uses for a stranger in his field.
annotation.definitionFit: To trespass is to push onto ground that is not yours, which is what encroaching is — both words describe a boundary quietly crossed.

indicatorNotes.wordplay for: Playing with a word means moving its letters about, so what follows is to be written out in a new order.

blocks.note: in British schools supply means filling in for an absent colleague — supply staff, working on supply
the seven letters of HECTARE rearranged

annotation.surface: A stand-in schoolteacher making a joke about the size of a hectare.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Temporary educator' looks like the definition entire; only the second word of it is, and the first is a piece of wordplay. A hectare is ten thousand square metres, but it is the letters and not the size that matter.
annotation.definitionFit: A supply teacher is brought in to cover an absent colleague and stands in front of the class all the same, which makes 'educator' plainly true.

entries.clue: Entrance in shelter for recipient of bequest (7)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' puts the thing just named inside the thing named next, one word swallowing the other.

blocks.note: the lee is the sheltered side, the one out of the wind
a gate is the entrance through a wall or a fence

annotation.surface: A gateway built into a shelter, left to whoever inherits.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lee' is the sheltered side of anything — a ship, a hedge, a hill — and it is the container here, split open after two of its three letters. 'Entrance' is the noun, not the verb meaning to enchant.
annotation.definitionFit: A legatee is the person a legacy is left to, the one named in the will who actually receives what was bequeathed.

blocks.note: a dull afternoon drags: the verb for time passing too slowly
and what drags, drags on — the phrase supplies its second word too

annotation.surface: Something that is starting to bore everybody present.
annotation.walkthrough: Four words with no instruction among them: a two-word phrase simply closes up into one. 'Drag on' is what a meeting does when nobody in the room will end it.
annotation.definitionFit: The fire-breathing winged serpent of legend is a mythical creature in the plainest sense of the phrase.

indicatorNotes.regularly ignored: Ignoring letters at regular intervals means dropping every other one, and what survives is read straight off in order.

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters of MIDDLEMAN'S

annotation.surface: Proposals from a go-between that everybody routinely disregards.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s counts as a letter to be stepped through, which makes the word ten long rather than nine. Extraction clues rarely say which of the two halves to keep, and the crossings decide it.
annotation.definitionFit: Plans are the schemes somebody puts forward, and ideas in this sense are the same thing — proposals offered for adoption rather than stray thoughts.

indicatorNotes.Content: The content of something is what sits inside it, so the letters wanted are held within the words that follow.

blocks.note: five letters running across the join, from inside FIND into RING

annotation.surface: Somebody perfectly happy to come across a ring-tailed lemur.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ring-tailed' belongs to a different lemur altogether, and here it is holding letters while pointing you at the wrong species. 'Content' is the noun stressed on its first syllable, not the adjective meaning pleased.
annotation.definitionFit: The indri is the largest of the Madagascan lemurs, a black-and-white tree-dweller with almost no tail at all.

entries.clue: Unite and get rid of duke (4)

blocks.note: to bin a thing is to throw it out, the bin being the British household rubbish basket
d = duke, the abbreviation used in titles

annotation.surface: An instruction to join forces and be done with the duke.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bin' as a verb is everyday British for throwing away and is doing almost all the work; the duke supplies only his initial. 'And' joins the definition to the wordplay and says nothing else.
annotation.definitionFit: To bind things is to tie them together into one, which is uniting them — the rope sense of the word rather than the legal one.

entries.clue: One’s allowed a little key, perhaps (5)

blocks.note: one is I in crossword numerals, and the 's that follows is written out as S
to let somebody do a thing is to allow it

annotation.surface: Somebody being permitted one small key of their own.
annotation.walkthrough: The key is not the door sort: off Florida and through the Caribbean a key, or cay, is a low sandy island. 'Perhaps' is the setter's warning that one is only an example of the other.
annotation.definitionFit: A key is a low island such as the Florida Keys, and a small island is an islet, with 'perhaps' marking the example.

blocks.note: what is in is what is fashionable and popular this season
Diana is the Roman goddess of hunting and the moon

annotation.surface: A report on the condition of a much-loved Roman goddess.
annotation.walkthrough: 'State of' reads as a condition, the state of the nation, and the first word alone is the definition with the second only joining. Diana is the Roman name for the Greek Artemis.
annotation.definitionFit: Indiana is one of the fifty American states, sitting in the Midwest with Indianapolis for its capital.

entries.clue: Beer losing head in high wind (3)

indicatorNotes.losing head: To lose your head is to lose the top of you, so the first letter of the word comes away.

blocks.note: a gale is a very strong wind; its leading G is the letter dropped

annotation.surface: A pint losing its froth to a storm.
annotation.walkthrough: The head of a beer is the froth on top, which the surface leans on while the instruction is about a letter. Ale is the older word of the two, from the days when beer meant only the hopped kind.
annotation.definitionFit: Ale is beer, the malt drink itself; the old distinction between the hopped and unhopped kinds has worn away and either word now serves.

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' says the letters are already sitting inside the words that follow, needing no assembly at all.

blocks.note: three letters crossing two gaps, from the end of AND through I to the start of PANIC

annotation.surface: Somebody jumping into the water and losing their nerve at once.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dive in' is so natural a phrase that the second word hides the instruction it is carrying. The run starts on the last letter of a word and crosses two gaps, which is the hardest shape of hiding place to see.
annotation.definitionFit: To take a dip is to go into the water for a quick swim, the everyday sense of 'dive' rather than the headfirst entry off a board.

entries.clue: Gets grime all over the place in kitchen items (3,6)

indicatorNotes.all over the place: What is all over the place is scattered out of any order, so the letters named are to be rearranged.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

annotation.surface: Dirt collecting everywhere across a kitchen.
annotation.walkthrough: Fodder and definition sit either side of the signal with nothing else in the clue at all. The thing itself is the little sand glass that runs for three minutes, or the dial version that pings.
annotation.definitionFit: An egg timer measures the few minutes a boiling egg needs, and lives in the kitchen drawer with the other small gadgets.
